blocks.html: In Chapter 2 we stored student records in files such as students.dat . That works for one small program. Now imagine a whole school using separate files:

items.html: the office keeps STUDENT.dat with roll number, name, class, address and phone;
the accounts section keeps FEES.dat with roll number, name, class, address and fee paid;
the library keeps LIBRARY.dat with roll number, name, class and the book issued.

blocks.html: This way of keeping data in separate files, each handled by its own program, is called a file system.

rows: The same data is stored again and again

"List students in Class 12 who have not paid fees and have a library book" needs code that reads all three files

One file is .dat , another is.csv , with different field orders

Library staff can open the fee file and see payments
Marks of 150 out of 100, or a fee record for a student who does not exist

blocks.html: A database is an organised collection of related data, stored together so that it can be accessed, managed and updated easily.

A Database Management System (DBMS) is software that creates and manages databases. It sits between users or programs and the stored data, and takes care of storage, retrieval, security, backup and consistency.

Popular DBMS software: MySQL, Oracle Database, PostgreSQL, Microsoft SQL Server, SQLite (used inside Android apps) and Microsoft Access. MongoDB is a popular NoSQL database that stores documents instead of tables.

blocks.html: The schema changes rarely, like the design of a building. The instance changes every day, like the people inside the building.
The most widely used way to organise a database is the relational model. It was proposed by E. F. Codd in 1970. Data is stored in tables, and in this model a table is called a relation.

A key is one or more attributes that uniquely identify each tuple in a relation, or that link one relation to another.
An attribute, or a minimal set of attributes, whose value is different for every tuple. A relation can have more than one candidate key.
In PATIENT, both PatientID and Phone are unique for each patient, so both are candidate keys. Name is not, because two patients can share a name.
The candidate key chosen by the database designer to identify the tuples. A primary key can never be NULL and can never repeat.
For PATIENT we choose PatientID as the primary key, because it is short, never changes, and is given by the clinic.
The candidate keys that were not chosen as the primary key. Here Phone is the alternate key.
Sometimes no single attribute is unique, but a combination is. Such a key is a composite key.
RollNo repeats and Date repeats, but (RollNo, Date) together is unique, so it is the composite primary key.
A foreign key is an attribute in one relation that refers to the primary key of another relation. It creates the link between the tables.

items.html: In APPOINTMENT, ApptID is the primary key.
PatientID is a foreign key that refers to PATIENT(PatientID).
DoctorID is a foreign key that refers to DOCTOR(DoctorID).

blocks.html: The patient's name and phone are not repeated in APPOINTMENT. They are stored once, in PATIENT, and reached through the foreign key. This removes the redundancy problem of the file system.
The DBMS makes sure that every foreign key value matches an existing primary key value in the referenced table, or is NULL. For example:

items.html: an appointment for patient P999 cannot be added, because P999 does not exist in PATIENT;
patient P101 cannot be deleted while appointments still refer to P101, unless the database is told what to do with those rows.

blocks.html: This rule is called referential integrity. It stops "orphan" records.

items.html: A file system keeps data in separate files, which leads to redundancy, inconsistency, difficult access, data dependence, and weak security and integrity.
A database is an organised collection of related data. A DBMS (MySQL, Oracle, PostgreSQL, SQLite) manages it.
Schema = the design. Instance = the data at one moment. Constraints = rules on the data. Metadata = data about the data. Query = a request for data.
In the relational model, data is stored in relations (tables) made of attributes (columns) and tuples (rows).
Domain = the allowed values of an attribute. Degree = the number of attributes. Cardinality = the number of tuples.
Values are atomic, tuples are distinct, the order of rows and columns does not matter, and NULL means unknown.
Candidate key: any minimal unique attribute set. Primary key: the chosen one (unique and never NULL). Alternate key: the other candidate keys. Composite key: a key of two or more attributes.
A foreign key refers to the primary key of another relation. Referential integrity keeps foreign keys valid.
